title: Why the Best Marriages Are Start-Ups, Not Mergers
author: Arthur C. Brooks
summary: Brooks takes a familiar social science finding, that the lowest five year divorce risk clusters around marrying between 28 and 32, and refuses to let it function as a verdict on anyone who missed the window. His move is to ask what the sweet spot is actually made of, then argue those conditions can be reconstructed at almost any age. The organizing metaphor is entrepreneurial: a good marriage behaves like a start-up founded by equals rather than a merger between two established firms with separate books and negotiated terms. From that he draws three practices. Pool the finances rather than maintaining separate accounts, because integration rather than accounting independence tracks with satisfaction. Abandon the fifty-fifty split, since strict equality crowds out generosity, which he treats as the load-bearing element of love. And think hard about what a prenuptial agreement wires into a partnership, given that asymmetric economic power makes corporate mergers difficult too. The piece opens with an extended comic riff on his wife's devotion to European cycling and his son's schoolyard breakfast sandwich arbitrage, which he uses to set up the entrepreneurship frame.
points: Brooks reframes the 28 to 32 optimal marriage age finding as a description of conditions to be re-created rather than a window that closes, explicitly including people at 72.
He argues that maintaining separate finances lowers the chance of success and that pooling funds should be the objective even for couples who have to get there gradually.
The case against a fifty-fifty split rests on generosity, which Brooks treats as the element of love that strict equality quietly suppresses.
He reads the fivefold rise in prenuptial agreements since 2010 as a prudence that may hardwire asymmetric economic power into the partnership.
The controlling image is co-founders who see each other as equals, which is what separates a start-up marriage from a merger between two established parties.
quotes: Many people have asked me when the optimal age to marry is. Social scientists have studied this. For example, a researcher at the Institute for Family Studies estimated that the optimal age for getting hitched is 28 to 32 for both partners.1 This is the “sweet spot,” where divorce within the first five years of marriage is lowest.

By looking at why the 28-to-32 bracket appears to work best, we might be able to re-create those conditions for almost any age—even 72. People who have passed the 28-to-32 window can benefit by resisting the characteristics of, to continue the business analogy, a corporate merger.

Corporate mergers struggle when financial integration is burdensome. The same goes for a marriage: Maintaining separate finances lowers the chances of success. Research shows that when couples pool their funds and learn to work together on saving and spending, they have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to split up.2

Worse, splitting things equally militates against one of the most important elements of love: generosity—a willingness to give more than your share in a spirit of abundance, because giving to someone you care for is pleasurable in itself.

A prenup might sound like simple prudence, but it is worth considering the asymmetric economic power dynamic that it can wire into the marriage. Some scholars have argued that this bodes ill for the partnership’s success, much as asymmetric economic power between two companies makes a merger difficult.4

But beyond all this, here’s the big thing to remember: Whether you are 22 or 72, the best approach to a successful love start-up is one in which co-founders see each other as equals and walk confidently into the future together in a spirit of generous, golden collaboration.

And in fact, the kids went on to be true entrepreneurs in short order, in what really counts the most: love. For example, both the boys had “start-up marriages” in their early twenties. And that’s my subject today.
